title: Product photography for a ceramics studio
metaTitle: Photography for a ceramics studio shop
excerpt: Shoot ceramics in the hand, with one crop and one background for the grid. Mixed frames make a careful studio look unfinished.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. Photography direction is a layout: one crop, one background, one brand.
caption: A layout decided before the files. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many photographs does a cup need?
faqs.answer: A hero on the shared background, a glaze detail, and an in-hand or in-use frame are enough for most cups. Add a group frame only when you sell the group. The hero also has to read at thumbnail size, or the collection page will fail even if the full image is beautiful.

faqs.question: Why do mixed crops matter in a small shop?
faqs.answer: The grid is where buyers compare glaze and form. Different angles, backgrounds, and margins make the shop look like several brands and hide the work. Storytelling images can live on the product page. The thumbnail should stay in the system.

faqs.question: What should alt text say?
faqs.answer: Describe the piece, the glaze, and the view, such as a stoneware cup in a green ash glaze held in a hand. Dimensions and care belong in the page text as well, so the facts are not trapped in the image. Do not stuff a search phrase into the alt text.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A ceramics studio product photography practice is a set of rules for crop, light, and background, plus a frame that shows the piece in a hand or on a table. The photograph has to carry glaze and scale, because the buyer cannot pick the cup up. Mixed crops in one grid make a careful studio look unfinished.

Photograph for the object in the hand. Keep the setup consistent enough that twenty pieces feel like one shelf. Then let the product page use those frames without inventing a new style per item.

## What the camera is responsible for

Words can carry dimensions, weight, and care. They cannot carry the break of a glaze or the thickness of a lip. Those are the photographs. Plan a small set per piece, and stop when the set is complete.

- A hero on the shared background, cropped the same way as the rest of the catalog.
- A detail of glaze or texture, tight enough to see variation, still in the same light.
- An in-hand or in-use frame that answers scale.
- A group frame only when you sell the group, so a set is not implied by accident.

Four is plenty for a cup. A vase might need a full-height frame instead of the in-hand shot, with a person or a table edge still in the frame so height is obvious. A platter needs the overhead and the edge. Write the set down per form. Do not rediscover it on shoot day for every piece, or the grid will drift.

The hero is what the collection page will shrink. If the hero only works when it is enormous, the grid will fail. Look at the hero at thumbnail size before you approve the set. The silhouette should read. A dark foot that disappears into a dark table will become a smudge in the category, and people will skip the piece for a reason that is not the work.

## One crop, one background, one light

Pick a background the glaze can live on. A warm paper, a pale stone, a painted wall you actually have. Use it for the heroes. Changing from marble to forest to pure white across one collection makes the shop look like three brands, even when one person threw every piece.

Pick a crop and a margin. If cups are shot from the same three-quarter angle with the same empty space on the left, the grid aligns and the eye compares glaze, which is what you want compared. If one cup is a tight square, the next is a wide scene, and the third is overhead, the grid is noisy. Occasional storytelling images can live on the product page or the journal. They should not be the thumbnail unless every thumbnail is a scene, which is a different system and a harder one to keep.

Light is the same idea. One direction, soft enough that the glaze is not a white blowout. Specular highlights on a glossy surface are part of the material. A highlight that clips to pure white is a lost glaze. Check the file, not only the camera screen.

Color is a promise. If the ash glaze is greener in the room than in the file, fix the file before it goes on the site. A buyer who receives a different color will not experience that as a minor grade. They will experience it as a different product. Shoot a known reference if you must, and look at the files on the kind of screen your buyers use, not only on a calibrated display in the studio. You will not control their phone. You can avoid the worst shifts.

## Scale without turning the photo into a lifestyle ad

The in-hand frame is doing a job. The hand is there so the cup's size is obvious. The hand is not there to sell a lifestyle, a season, or a model's wardrobe. Keep clothing plain. Keep the table the buyer will understand. A styled picnic that hides the foot of the bowl has failed the brief even if it is a beautiful picture.

If you would rather not use hands, use one repeatable reference: a standard plate, a spoon, the edge of a book. Use the same reference across the catalog so the sizes relate to each other. Switching from a hand to a cathedral step to a coin is the mixed-crop problem in another form.

Groups are where scale lies by accident. Three small cups cropped tight can look like bowls. Pull back until the table is visible, or do not use the group as the hero. The hero can be one piece. The group can be the second image.

Say the dimensions in text anyway. A photograph suggests scale. The numbers confirm it. The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) asks for a text alternative on images. The alt text should describe the piece, the glaze, and the view, not the keyword you hope to rank for. "Stoneware cup in a green ash glaze, held in a hand" is alt text. A caption can carry the dimensions again for people who will not find them in a tab. The W3C's principles, perceivable and understandable among them, are the right test: the image is not the only place the facts exist.

## Files that do not wreck the page

Large photographs are often the largest thing on the page, which means they decide how fast the product appears. Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) guidance asks for Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. A hero that arrives late, or that shoves the price down when it finally loads, fails that bar. Export the size the template actually displays. Reserve the space in the layout so the page does not jump. Do not upload the camera original and hope the shop resizes it kindly.

Keep a naming scheme the studio will follow: form, glaze, view. "final-FINAL-2.jpg" will be the wrong glaze on the page by next month. The next firing should be able to drop files into the same slots.

Retouch dust and obvious crumbs. Do not retouch the glaze into a smoothness the pot does not have. The buyer is paying for this clay and this firing. A plastic surface will increase disappointment, and it will make the in-hand photo and the hero look like different objects.

If you sell the same form in several glazes, shoot them together in one session. Matching light a month later is harder than it sounds, and the grid will show the mismatch as a quality problem in the work rather than in the files.

## The grid is the test

Lay the heroes out in the real category template before you call the shoot done. Look for the piece that is brighter, tighter, or more shadowed than its neighbors. Reshoot or regrade that one. A single mismatched tile is what makes the shop feel unfinished, more than any sentence on the page.

Check the sold and the small states. A crop that looks balanced at full size may put the cup under the price label on the grid. Adjust the margin as a system, not by nudging one image until that one product looks fine and the next one does not.

Thumbnails are also what people use when they return to compare two glazes. If the two heroes were shot on different days with different warmth, they will choose the file, not the pot. Consistency is a fairness to the work.

When a new series needs a different background, change the whole series and the template together, or keep the old background until you can reshoot. A half-migrated grid is the mixed look you are trying to avoid. Do it between collections, not in the middle of a Friday upload.

An [intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) is enough to look at a handful of current files and say whether the grid problem is crop, light, or the template fighting the pictures. Bring the category page, not a mood board.

## What not to photograph

Do not photograph a stand-in piece and sell a different one from the same batch if the glaze varies. Either the variation is the point and you show the actual piece, or the batch is consistent and you say so. Do not steal scale by shooting with a wide lens close to the object so it looms. The distortion reads as clumsiness once the piece arrives.

Do not cover the lip, the foot, or the handle with props. Those are the parts a potter judges, and they are the parts a buyer gets wrong when they cannot be seen. Flowers in a vase are fine as a second frame if the rim is still visible somewhere in the set. They are a poor hero when the flowers are the subject.

Avoid text burned into the image: prices, "handmade," badges. Text in the photograph cannot be translated, updated, or read reliably by assistive technology. Put those words in the page. The photograph stays the object.

Keep a contact sheet of rejected frames with a note on why, if several people shoot. "Too tight," "background drifted," "glaze clipped." The note is how the next session matches this one without a meeting.

## Direction the studio can keep using

Write one page of direction: background, angle per form, the four-frame set, the alt-text pattern, the export size. The person who throws the pots may not be the person who photographs them next year. The page is what keeps the shop looking like itself.

Revisit the direction when you add a new form. A lamp is not a cup with a taller crop. Give it its own row in the direction, then hold that row still. The discipline is the same one the shop needs in its templates. The files and the pages either agree, or the buyer feels the seam.

Clothing has the same seam, with a different subject. [An online shop for a clothing label](/blog/an-online-shop-for-a-clothing-label) is the next piece, because fabric, fit, and a body replace glaze and a hand, and the checkout is still the short part at the end.
